# Deterrence (`deterrence`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by game_theory, security_dilemma_arms_race, nuclear_weapons, military_intelligence_codebreaking
- Core idea: Prevent attack by convincing the opponent beforehand that it will cost more than it can gain, either because it will fail (denial) or because retaliation will follow (punishment). It works through his mind, so three things are needed: the capability, a believable will to use it (credibility), and clear communication of what is forbidden, together with the assurance that he will be left alone if he refrains. With nuclear weapons the capability must survive a first blow (second strike): if both sides can still destroy the other after being attacked, neither gains by striking first (mutual assured destruction). Credibility is the hard part, above all when protecting an ally; commitments are made believable by treaties, troops stationed in harm's way and reputation.
- Pitfalls:
  - Deterrence is not the same as defence or as strength; forces that can be destroyed in a surprise attack invite it
  - Threats that are too terrible to carry out are not believed for small provocations, so the opponent advances in small slices
  - It assumes the opponent calculates, values survival and understands the signal; it fails through misperception, desperation, accident and false alarm (1962, 1983)
  - A threat without an assurance leaves the opponent nothing to lose
  - 'If you want peace, prepare for war' ignores that preparations can frighten the neighbour into arming or striking first
  - It gives no way out when it fails, and a long peace does not prove that it was the cause
- History: greece: 433 BC – Athens makes a purely defensive alliance with Corcyra to deter Corinth, and fails (Thucydides I.44–55); 427 BC – Diodotus argues that the threat of death does not deter rebels because hope outweighs fear (III.45); 416 BC – Melian dialogue; china: c. 5th–4th c. BC – Sun Tzu: the highest skill is to subdue the enemy without fighting and to make oneself unassailable; india: c. 1st c. BC – 3rd c. AD – Arthashastra: the ruler's coercive power (danda) and visible readiness keep rivals quiet; rome: c. AD 400 – Vegetius III, preface: 'whoever wants peace should prepare for war'; Roman policy of certain and exemplary retaliation; europe: 1454 – Italian League deters by promised joint action; 17th–18th c. – fortress belts and 'fleets in being' deter by denial; global: 1946 – Bernard Brodie: the chief purpose of armed forces is now to avert wars; 1959 – Wohlstetter on vulnerable deterrent forces; 1960–1966 – Schelling on commitment and credibility; 1960s – assured destruction (McNamara), nicknamed MAD by its critic Donald Brennan; 1962 – Cuban missile crisis
- Read:
  - Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War I.31–55, III.37–48, V.84–116
  - Thomas C. Schelling, Arms and Influence (1966)
  - Lawrence Freedman, The Evolution of Nuclear Strategy (1981)
